messages.subject: signal to noise ratio
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I want to calculate signal to noise ratio for songs to be able to filter the ones of bad quality. I would like to do it following the formula in this paper:

Gasc, Amandine, et al. "Assessing biodiversity with sound: Do acoustic diversity indices reflect phylogenetic and functional diversities of bird communities?." Ecological Indicators 25 (2013): 279-287.

They report this formula:

SNR = 100 × ( rms ( S ) /rms ( N )), where S and N are the probability mass functions of the amplitude envelope of 0.5 s of signal and of 0.5 s of noise both randomly chosen along the recording considered, respectively, and rms is the root mean square

My question is: Does anyone know how can I do this with seewave?

Cheers

John

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] signal to noise ratio
messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

Just to add to Thomas' comment, the env and rms functions should do what you want. However, you may also want to consider that in most practical applications, when we measure 'signal' we're actually measuring both signal and noise (as it's impossible to separate the two in a recording). i.e. I would argue that your S would actually be S+N.

In my work I calculated SNR like this:
SN <- env(signal_in_noise)
N <- env(noise)
SNR <- (rms(SN) - rms(N))/rms(N)

And you could always multiply the SNR by 100, too. Good luck!

Steffi
Dr. Stefanie LaZerte
Natural Resources and Environmental Studies
University of Northern BC
stefanie...@unbc.ca
http://steffi.ca/

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] signal to noise ratio
messages.body_plain:
I think they should have the same duration (ideally), but it may not be strictly necessary.

If I remember (and understand) correctly, the rms can be considered "average" sound power, so the the rms' values calculated from segments of different lengths should be comparable. However, I don't think this is a good idea, you'd be better off sticking to the same duration.

Steffi

Natural Resources and Environmental Studies
University of Northern BC

Hi Sean,

When I do a quick search for these filters in R:
help.search("butter")
I get hits suggesting that the butter and buttord functions can be found in the signal package and that the bwfilter is in the seewave package.

Have you made sure to load the relevant libraries before starting?
library(seewave)
library(signal)

Whenever I see the "'x' function not found" error message 99% of the time it's because I hadn't loaded the library when I thought I did.

messages.subject_clean: help with automated multispecies analysis of large recording data
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,
My name is Hemant and I recently joined this group. I have been exploring acoustic ecology since last few weeks.

Slightly different query here...
I am fascinated by the idea of detecting multiple species and generating species lists from long term recordings using known species templates. I found monitoR package by Katz et al. 2015 which can probably do that. I test ran it by downloading known species songs from XenoCanto and used a 24 hour recording i made in a garden here as a survey file from which I need to detect species.
In my templates somehow I see that lowest amplitude is shown as -inf and maximum as 0. I dont understand what that means.

 The results show that all the species (5 species templates) are present which does not make sense as one of the species that I used is not found in this country.
I am new to acoustic ecology and may be I did not understand some of the key steps. I feel the amplitude cutoff that I used i.e. -41 may be creating some problems. Can someone please explain me how this works?
I will be very glad.

Thank you in advance,
Hemant Tripathi

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] signal to noise ratio
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I think the thing is not so much to have equal samples of noise and of signal+noise but the have enough data points for each for the rms values to asymptotically approach a "true" value. This may be a problem if the signal amplitude varies rapidly as it may do with bird song.

Also, in my field recordings the signal is often so weak that a (spikey) time domain spectrum does not permit a clear distinction between periods of signal and periods of noise only. In such cases I find it preferable to use aggregate powers between appropriate frequency bands instead. Note, the aggregate power (on a linear, not db, scale) over a range of frequency bands at a given time is a linear function of the squared amplitude - smoothed over the DFT window length and weighted according the the window weighting (Hann, Hamming...).

I am afraid I have no scripts to offer as I use my own, homemade software (in C++) for such things.

Krzysz

messages.subject: ACI bizzare values (and uncertainty about H/Ht/Hf indices)
messages.subject_clean: ACI bizzare values (and uncertainty about H/Ht/Hf indices)
messages.body_plain:
Hey guys,

I'm using indices in Seewave to determine underwater acoustic differences between sites. I've taken 45min recordings four times per day (midday, dusk, midnight and dawn) for comparisons. Files are in 15min blocks, 96kHz sample rate and 24bit wav. ACI is calculated on each minute of the recording.

I've attached a screenshot of the spectrogram in audacity of a recording from one site, a snippet from midday in the top channel and from midnight in the bottom channel. There is clearly a lot of difference - a lot more insect noise (6-11kHz) in midnight than midday, yet ACI values show very little variation; and in fact the mean ACI for the 45 mins of recording at midday is higher than mean ACI of the midnight recording: 67.00872 ± 2.48 midday cf. 65.75283 ± 1.38 for midnight (Site 4; mean ± 1 SD). Ive also included a box plot of the ACI values.

All ACI settings are the default at the moment, other than frequency limits (0.5-20kHz).

I would expect the midnight values to be significantly higher than midnight. Can anyone explain why I might be getting these odd values? Is 1min too long to be calculating ACI values for underwater sounds?
My concern is that if there is an issue with these values between time of day when there is known variation, then any acoustic variation that exists between sites is most likely also being missed.

Additionally, I was also interested in using the H or Hf indices, however I am hoping someone might be able to teach me how to "set" them properly.
If I use the default settings built in to seewave, H  ≠ Ht * Hf, and all H/Ht/Hf values are very high - circa 0.97-0.98.  While the SNR is low for underwater recordings, I did not expect it to show values this high. The files have not had any noise reduction applied, however if noise reduction is applied values are still > 0.95. Filtering the low frequencies out (wind) < 0.5kHz lowers the values to around 0.94.

I have tried many combinations of settings for all 3 indices, however I still cannot make them equal. Any suggestions would be appreciated.

Cheers,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] ACI bizzare values (and uncertainty about H/Ht/Hf indices)
messages.subject_clean: [seewave] ACI bizzare values (and uncertainty about H/Ht/Hf indices)
messages.body_plain:
Dear Chris,

Regarding ACI: the ACI was designed to be sensitive to bird acoustic diversity with important FMs and AMs and to resist at the same time to continuous noise such as engine noises. Here you seem to have insect stridulations with a regular pattern that might not be caught by ACI. But please take contact with the degsiners of the index for proper comments.

Regarding H, Ht, Hf: it is true that H-like indices reach quite quickly high values in particular for noise-like sound as aquatic insect stridulation do. For more information on Hf and Ht in aquatic environments see https://peerj.com/articles/1393/

Here is a test of the computation of H, Hf and Ht that seems to be consistent.
> data(tico)
> Ht <- th(env(tico, plot=FALSE))
> Hf <- sh(meanspec(tico, plot=FALSE))
> Ht*Hf
[1] 0.6627356
> H(tico)
[1] 0.6627356

HTH

Best regards,

Jerome
